summary: Pinnacle Peak near Enumclaw: a 1929 pole lookout, removed by tractor in 1966, and a 33-foot replica finished on the summit in 2021.

facts.design: Replica of the lookout removed in 1966

access.note: County park with trails to the summit. The sources read do not confirm the replica is open today; check with King County Parks.

visit.trail_note: Cal Magnusson Trail climbs 1,000 feet in a mile; the South Trail is an old gravel road that mountain bikes share

events.note: aircraft warning station on the summit during WWII
last full-time observer was Linda Makela
tower pulled down by tractor on May 13
replica tower finished in late October

evidence.supports: 30-foot pole tower in 1929, replaced by a 60-foot tower in 1934
evidence.quote: In 1929, a 30-foot pole tower was constructed near the top of Pinnacle Peak and replaced in 1934 by a 60-foot tower.

evidence.supports: trails first built to reach a state Division of Forestry lookout (county trail page quotes a local historian)
evidence.quote: The trails were first built to access a State Division of Forestry (now Washington Department of Natural Resources) lookout tower.

evidence.supports: Washington Forest Fire Association built the 1929 and 1934 towers
evidence.quote: In May 1929 a 30 foot pole platform tower was built by the Washington Forest Fire Association. In 1934 the WFFA constructed a higher 60 foot tower.

evidence.supports: WTA dates the lookout name to 1928 to 1971 (conflicts with 1929 and 1966)
evidence.quote: Between 1928 and 1971, a fire lookout perched atop the mountain was called the Pinnacle Peak Lookout

evidence.supports: park is 335 acres on a volcanic cone one mile southeast of Enumclaw
evidence.quote: Pinnacle Peak Park is a 335-acre volcanic cone one mile southeast of downtown Enumclaw

evidence.supports: 1942 aircraft warning station on the summit
evidence.quote: In 1942, an Aircraft Warning Station was located atop Pinnacle Peak with the mission of spotting enemy aircraft during WWII.

evidence.supports: at least 30 staff; last full-time observer Linda Makela in 1964
evidence.quote: At least 30 men and women staffed the lookouts over the years with the last full time observer being a White River High School graduate, Linda Makela in 1964.

evidence.supports: tower manned four days in 1965
evidence.quote: But, the tower was again manned 4 days in 1965 on March 13, 14, 20 and 21.

evidence.supports: tower pulled down by Caterpillar tractor on May 13, 1966
evidence.quote: At 11 a.m., May 13, 1966 a Caterpillar tractor pulled down the Pinnacle Peak lookout tower, ending 37 years of fire detection service.

evidence.supports: torn down May 13, 1966 with a tractor
evidence.quote: It was torn down May 13, 1966 with a D-4 caterpiller tractor at 11:00 A.M.

evidence.supports: removal reason: vandalism, break-ins and risk to children
evidence.quote: the tower suffered so much vandalism and break-ins it was necessary to remove it to prevent a serious accident to children playing on the tower.

evidence.supports: concrete footings of the old lookout at the top of the peak
evidence.quote: the old concrete footings of a long-gone fire lookout

evidence.supports: replica is 33 feet tall and copies the structure on the same spot decommissioned in 1966
evidence.quote: The 33-foot-tall lookout tower is a replica of the structure that once stood on the same spot until it was decommissioned by the Washington Department of Natural Resources in 1966.

evidence.supports: replica work finished
evidence.quote: Work on the new Mount Peak fire tower is now finished.

evidence.quote: Posted Fri, Oct 29, 2021 at 1:24 pm PT

evidence.quote: an optional 22-foot climb to the viewing deck

notes_for_editor: Dates conflict: the WTA hike page gives the lookout's name as 1928 to 1971; the county and the Willhite history give a 1929 build and a May 1966 removal. The story uses 1929 and 1966. The 1929 builder is attributed differently: the county says the trails served a state Division of Forestry lookout; Willhite says the Washington Forest Fire Association built both towers. Height: Patch reports 33 feet; an undated cached history page (data/raw/web/88dea7fe3b3599da9b8a31e5fb1fd2ee5fd38837.bin, no URL recovered) gives 20 feet for the replica. That page is not cited. The King County news release and the King County Parks blog post returned 404 and are not cited. Opening status in 2026 is unconfirmed. The WTA trail-closure notice is dated 10.13.26; the only valid US reading is October 13, 2026, and the story now gives that date. The 1928 to 1971 WTA range is now described as differing from the 1929 build and 1966 removal dates, rather than as contradicting them. The footings sentence and the Patch 'copy' sentence were reworded so they no longer copy source text; no claim was removed.
